(2026) 207:247
https://doi.org/10.1007/s11229-026-05639-1
ORIGINAL RESEARCH

Why the definition of determinism fails and how it can be
corrected: the case of classical particle mechanics
Antoni Antoszek1
Received: 29 June 2025 / Accepted: 6 May 2026
© The Author(s) 2026

Abstract
This paper aims to demonstrate how a rigorous definition of determinism can be
formulated and applied to a formal axiomatization of a physical theory. Examining
an example of Newtonian classical particle mechanics (CPM) formalized in set-theoretical axioms by Patrick Suppes, the paper shows why definitions of determinism
based on the temporal development of physical systems—such as those proposed
by Suppes (2002) and Montague (1974)—fail to assess determinism correctly. It is
argued that, to deliver a meaningful verdict, the definition of determinism cannot
be applied to the entire framework of CPM itself, but rather to its particular theories: definitions of specific physical systems that incorporate the force equation.
Therefore, the verdict of determinism or indeterminism typically depends on the
uniqueness (or non-uniqueness) of solutions to the differential equations governing the system’s behavior. The paper concludes with a demonstration of how a
formally correct definition of determinism can be used to show the indeterminism
of the theory of Norton’s dome stated within the framework of CPM. Although the
example concerns pre-relativistic Newtonian mechanics, the crucial philosophical
distinction between frameworks and theories extends beyond this case and suggests
that assessing the determinism of any physical theory requires special caution to
distinguish it properly from its framework.
Keywords Classical particle mechanics · Determinism · Norton’s dome · Physical
frameworks · Physical theories

Antoni Antoszek
ant.antoszek@student.uj.edu.pl
1

Jagiellonian University, Kraków, Poland

1 Introduction
Is classical particle mechanics (CPM) deterministic? One way to address this question is to formalize CPM using first-order or set-theoretical axioms and then test
whether certain initial conditions allow multiple temporal developments. This task
has been undertaken by Richard Montague (1974) and Patrick Suppes (2002), who
axiomatized CPM in first-order logic and set-theory, respectively. They both claimed
that the question of determinism is almost trivial – yet, they were led to entirely different results. As Montague claims:
We may now ask whether classical particle mechanics is deterministic, as is
sometimes alleged. According to the following theorem, whose proof is too
obvious to be included, the answer is negative.
Theorem 2. [C]PM is not deterministic. (Montague, 1974, p. 330)
On the other hand, examining his axiomatization of CPM, Suppes states that:
The next theorem is a classic expression of the fact that particle mechanics is a
thoroughly deterministic science … The proof rests upon elementary considerations concerning the uniqueness of solutions of the kind of differential equation exemplified by Newton’s Second Law and is thus omitted here. (Suppes,
2002, p. 324)
Skipping a proof due to its alleged simplicity is generally unwise, so it may seem
that at least one of the authors made a mistake that led him to incorrect conclusions.
However, it turns out that both theorems are formally correct. More surprisingly, this
discrepancy does not arise from the differences in the choice of the formal language
either (a point that will be elaborated on in the next sections). Instead, the fundamental issue lies in the definition of determinism itself: in their texts, Montague and Suppes conceived of determinism in distinct ways, which in turn led them to divergent
conclusions.
The purpose of this article is to discuss how an appropriate definition of determinism can be formulated and applied to an axiomatization of classical particle mechanics. While drawing on Montague’s idea of determinism, later developed by Earman,
we argue that in order to deliver a meaningful verdict, a definition of determinism
should not be applied to the entire framework of classical particle mechanics, but
rather to its particular theories describing different physical systems. To demonstrate
this, we will examine why both Suppes’ and Montague’s (Earman’s) approaches fail.
This paper focuses on the DMAP approach to defining determinism that takes into
account temporal developments of different realizations of a theory and the existence
of suitable mappings between them (hence the name coined by Müller and Placek,
2018). In Sect. 2, we will examine several attempts – some of which remain informal – to construct a DMAP-style definition of determinism, together with the basic
terminology used by the proponents of these approaches. It will then be applied to
Suppes’ formalization of CPM, whose axiomatic structure will be laid down and dis-

13

Synthese

(2026) 207:247

Page 3 of 24

247

cussed in Sect. 3. Section 4 will examine why Suppes’ verdict that his axiomatization
of CPM is deterministic is premature. The failure of his approach suggests the need
to develop a new formal definition of determinism that follows the DMAP analysis
and makes it applicable to the set-theoretical formalization of CPM. This will be done
in Sect. 5. Although this definition is formally correct and consistent with DMAP, it
ultimately fails, prompting further analysis: how can we meaningfully apply it to the
framework? It will be argued that this can be done by asking about determinism of
theories of a framework rather than of a framework itself; the distinction between
theories and frameworks will be elaborated on in Sect. 6. Finally, in Sect. 7, we will
demonstrate an application of the revised definition to the theory of Norton’s (2008)
domes that is stated within the framework of classical particle mechanics. Assuming
that a framework is indeterministic when any of its theories are, this analysis will lead
to the verdict of indeterminism of classical particle mechanics.

2 When is a theory deterministic?
As Müller and Placek (2018) put it, “the core idea behind the philosophical (metaphysical) notion of determinism is that given the way things are at present, there
is only one possible way for the future to turn out’. The authors characterize three
approaches to defining determinism, including a ‘current orthodoxy in philosophy
of science” – a formulation examining mappings between temporal realizations of a
theory. The authors define this mapping-based approach, called DMAP analysis, as
follows:
Speaking abstractly, the diagnosis of determinism according to DMAP is a twostage affair. In a first step, all of the individual realizations of the linear temporal
development of systems falling under the theory are put side by side. These are
the separate possible ways a world could be that are admitted by the theory.
Depending on the theory in question, these could be all the solutions to the
theory’s defining equations, or a class of temporal realizations that is given in
some other, perhaps more complex manner … In a second step, this class of
temporal developments is checked for instances of indeterminism, in the following way: If there are two realizations that can be identified at one time, but
whose future segments after that time cannot be identified, this signals indeterminism. If the test fails, that is, if all realizations that can be identified at one
time can also be identified at all future times, then the theory is deterministic.
(Müller & Placek, 2018)
In the above description, key notions such as “theory”, “realization”, and “agreeing’
remain ambiguous and are interpreted differently by philosophers. In his entry in
the Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Jeremy Butterfield, a proponent of the
DMAP approach, claims that “a theory is deterministic if and only if: any two of
its models that agree at a time t on the state of their objects, also agree at all times
future to t” (Butterfield, 2005). A model, corresponding to what Müller and Placek
call a “realization”, is defined for theories describing single isolated systems to be a

13

247

Page 4 of 24

Synthese

(2026) 207:247

‘sequence of states for such a single system, that conforms to the laws of the theory’.
Therefore, it does not have to be a model in a strictly logical Tarskian sense, but
rather, as Butterfield puts it, a “toy universe” or a ‘toy possible world”. The concept
of “state” in Butterfield’s definition remains imprecise. States are required only to
have two general features that “are vague, and cannot be formalized’: they must be
‘intrinsic properties”1 and they must be maximal, “that is they need to be the logically strongest consistent properties the theory can express” (Butterfield, 2005). Two
models agree when their instantaneous slices are isomorphic. The application of isomorphism to such general models is problematic – after all, neither the structure nor
the language of such models is specified.
A slightly different route to define determinism in a DMAP approach is taken by
Earman:
In pre-QM physics it was also assumed that there is a set O of genuine physical
magnitudes (a.k.a. “observables”) each of which takes a determinate value at
every moment of time; call these the occurent magnitudes … A history H is a
map from R to tuples of values of the basic magnitudes, where for any t ∈ R
the state H(t) gives a snapshot of behavior of the basic magnitudes at time t.
The world is Laplacian deterministic with respect to O just in case for any pair
of histories H1 , H2 satisfying the laws of physics, if H1 (t) = H2 (t) for some t,
then H1 (t) = H2 (t) for all t. (Earman, 2007, pp. 1369–1370)
Here, realizations are histories, i.e. mappings from R to O; “agreeing” is understood
as equality. One concern is that Earman’s definition applies to the world rather than to
a theory, but this does not seem to be a real problem: it is natural to interpret histories
as realizations of certain physical theories describing the world. What is understood
by Butterfield as an instantaneous slice at time t, here can be seen simply as H(t), i.e.
a state or a tuple of physical magnitudes at time t. Thus, both authors are concerned
about states of a system, either ordered by some type of sequence (Butterfield) or by
arguments of a function (Earman). Note that in Earman’s formulation, the notion of
isomorphism is replaced by simple equality.2
1

Butterfield elaborates on this point:
It is notoriously hard to say exactly what is meant by ‘intrinsic’, but the idea is to rule out properties
which might code information about how the future just happens to go, and thus support a spurious
determinism. Thus, to take an everyday example, ‘Fred was mortally wounded at noon’ implies that
Fred later dies. But the property ascribed at noon is clearly extrinsic: it ‘looks ahead’ to the future.
And so this implication does not show that there is any genuine determinism about the processes
that led to Fred’s later death (Butterfield, 2005).

2

Throughout this text, we will discuss and formulate definitions that use set-theoretical identity “=” rather
than isomorphism when identifying “sameness” of models. As some authors (see Butterfield, 1989)
believe that identity is unreliable in this case, this choice might seem to be controversial. However, in the
case of classical particle mechanics to which the definition is applied, switching to isomorophism does
not appear to have any significant consequences beyond making the definition more complex. In the case
of other theories (or – as will be later argued – frameworks) such as general relativity, there seems to be
general consensus, backed with the famous Hole Argument, that the models are the same when they are
isomorophic. For the purposes of this text, identity is sufficient; however, it should be clear that it can be
straightforwardly replaced by isomorphism, most importantly in Definition 6 (Sect. 6).

13

Synthese

(2026) 207:247

Page 5 of 24

247

This approach will turn out to be very useful. If a theory is deterministic according
to Earman’s definition, we will say that it is Laplacian deterministic.
The notion of a theory remains insufficiently precise in either Butterfield’s or Earman’s formulation. One of the purposes of this text is to show that in order to use
DMAP analysis correctly, it is necessary to carefully specify what a physical theory
is and what it is not. Examining the case of classical particle mechanics, we will
argue that it is not meaningful to apply DMAP formulation to the whole Newtonian
framework, but rather to its particular theories.
A DMAP analysis requires a theory to be formulated in a precise scientific language that will allow us to find a class of realizations that is admitted by this theory.
It is not necessary to construct a new formalization of CPM: a set-theoretical axiomatization of CPM proposed by Suppes (2002, pp. 313–324) will be sufficient for
the purpose of this text. After introducing the formalization, we will examine Suppes’
theorem which claims that CPM is a deterministic theory. Although the theorem is
formally correct, the underlying definition of determinism is inadequate. To correct
it, we will demonstrate that the definition of Laplacian determinism can be applied
to Suppes’ formalization. The result of such application will illustrate that although
CPM may seem to be a physical theory, we must complement it with additional axioms that allow us to assess determinism in a way that is non-trivial and meaningful.
It may be asked why the focus is on the DMAP approach when studying the solutions to the differential equations seems to be sufficient for delivering a verdict on
determinism of CPM. There is a historical reason for this: both Butterfield’s and
Earman’s influential definitions cited before view determinism as an issue of mappings between temporal developments.3 This has been grounded in a rich tradition
of applying DMAP-type analysis to the determinism of physical theories, including
CPM, ranging from Montague and Suppes to the very recent arguments such as those
given by Halvorson et al. (2026).
There is also a conceptual reason for focusing on the DMAP approach. We believe
it is sufficiently general to cover theories where analyzing the solutions to the differential equation alone is inadequate (e.g., quantum mechanics, where the Schrödinger
equation is formally deterministic, but analyzing it in isolation fails to account for
the theory’s inherent indeterminacy upon measurement). It also might happen that
the initial value problem has unique solutions up to a gauge transformation; then
the purported instances of indeterminism are merely different representations of the
same physical scenario (for an example, see Earman, 2002). In practice, DMAP still
assigns a great importance to the well-posedness of the initial value problem whenever possible. This philosophically general approach can almost always satisfactorily
spell the very idea of determinism but at the same time recognizes the importance of
differential equations. Thus, we perform our analysis, especially in Sect. 7, fully in
the lines of the ‘marks of the current orthodoxy’, where (1) a theory is represented by
its realizations; (2) the question of determinism is spelled out in terms of mappings
between realizations; (3) we check for an agreement of physical states of the system;

3

DMAP is also a standard way of understanding determinism in encyclopedia entries (see e.g. Bishop,
2006; Hoefer, 2024).

13

247

Page 6 of 24

Synthese

(2026) 207:247

(4) and practical assessment depends mostly on the behavior of defining differential
equations (Müller & Placek, 2018, pp. 13–14).
It must be noted that the pioneering analysis of determinism according to the
DMAP approach was proposed by Montague (1974), who built a highly formal definition of determinism and applied it to his first-order axiomatization of classical
particle mechanics. Years later, Earman followed Montague’s general idea, modifying his definition slightly to make it applicable to theories that are not necessarily
formalized according to particular rules given by Montague.4 Many sections of this
text follow Montague’s method; in particular, it turns out that different approaches
to defining determinism deliver the same verdict on determinism or indeterminism
of set-theoretical axioms of CPM as they did in the case of Montague’s first-order
formalization.

3 Systems of classical particle mechanics – a set-theoretical
approach
Let us begin by presenting the definition of the set-theoretical predicate ‘is a system
of classical particle mechanics’ proposed by Suppes. Some non-essential difficulties
with this formalization are discussed in the footnotes.
First, the notion of a set-theoretical predicate requires clarification. Suppes’
famous slogan is “to axiomatize a theory is to define a set-theoretical predicate”
(Suppes, 2002, p. 30). However, an immediate tension arises between “axiomatizing” and ‘‘defining”, since proper definitions should be conservative and eliminable,
unlike axioms.5 A set-theoretical predicate is one definable within set theory, ultimately using only the ∈ relation, although in such definitions many abbreviations
may appear. It follows that “axiomatizing” a theory does not involve construing axioms in a strict logical sense. Consider Suppes’ example of the definition of the predicate “is a group”:
(A1) x ◦ (y ◦ z) = (x ◦ y) ◦ z.
(A2) x ◦ e = x.
(A3) x ◦ x−1 = e.

Definition 1 A is a group iff there exists a nonempty set A, a binary operation ◦ on A,
an element e of A and an inverse operation −1 on A such that A = (A, ◦, e,−1 ) and
for every x, y, z ∈ A the three axioms given above are satisfied. (Suppes, 2002, p. 31)
4

Consequently, Earman’s definition is less formal than Montague’s one. For example, Montague’s formalization of classical particle mechanics allows to treat “time” purely syntactically, i.e. simply as the first
argument of some functions. Indeed, Montague’s definition can be formulated without reference to any
informal understanding of time.

5

For an explanation of those criteria, see Belnap (1993).

13

Synthese

(2026) 207:247

Page 7 of 24

247

Here, we do not “axiomatize” a theory by introducing new primitive notions, providing the axioms that describe their behavior, and claiming that each Tarskian model
of such a theory is a group. Rather, we simply define that a certain tuple is a group
iff there exists a set, two operations, and a constant (all understood set-theoretically)
such that certain formulas are satisfied. While the only real axioms that may be mentioned in this case are the ones of set-theory, we will often claim that the sentences
describing some notions (formally being a part of the definition) are “axioms” in the
semi-formal sense described above. In fact, observe that this was exactly the case in
the above definition of a group. In Suppes’ words:
The difficulty with these axioms, taken in isolation, is that one does not quite
understand how they are related to other axioms of other theories, or exactly
how they are related to mathematical objects themselves. These uncertainties
are easily cleared up by recognizing that in essence the axioms are part of a
definition, namely, the definition of the predicate ‘is a group’. The axioms are
the most important part of the definition of this predicate, because they tell us
the most important properties that must be possessed by a mathematical object
which satisfies the predicate ‘is a group’, or in other words, by a mathematical
object that is a group. (Suppes, 2002, p. 31)
Throughout, we use ‘‘structure” or ‘‘model” to mean a tuple satisfying the relevant
predicate (unless we explicitly say otherwise). The term ‘‘realizations”, used by some
proponents of DMAP, is more appropriate here, as this way we do not confuse them
with models in Tarskian sense. A theory will be understood as a definition of a settheoretical predicate.
Suppes’ aim is to state classical particle mechanics in the language of set theory.6
The major difference between this formalization and the one presented by McKinsey
et al. (1953) is that positions are represented as points in an affine space rather than
vectors in a three-dimensional real space.7 Suppes argues that this makes the representation more coordinate-free.
6

This is clearly not the only way to go. Another approach would be to introduce the new primitive notions
within the first-order logic and then claim that classical particle mechanics is a set of some sentences in
this language, i.e. a theory in the logical sense. This route is taken by Montague (1974), whose “systems”
(in his terminology: histories) of CPM are Tarskian models of a logical theory in a first-order language.
The main difficulty of a ‘standard formalization’, as Suppes labels this approach, is that all mathematical
concpets that are needed must be introduced explicitly by first-order axioms. Observe that this is highly
inconvenient when we speak about a function being differentiable or about a convergent series (as we will
do soon); for instance, to handle the first case, Montague defines the second derivative of some particular
functions rather than define the second derivative in general. However, it must be noted that standard formalizations have other merits: although sometimes we want to use some mathematical concepts, assuming all facts about sets might be too much. This is precisely the account of Andréka et al. (2002) who in
an unpublished book on axiomatizing relativity theories in a first-order language claim that while in set
theory the truth or falsity of a predicate ⊨ is sometimes dependent on the whole set-theoretical universe,
the first-order logic is free from such a pathology (for a more elaborate discussion on this point, see
Andréka et al. 2002, pp. 1245–1252).

7

This is the difference that is stressed by Suppes himself. Other than that, the formalization from 1953
does not distinguish from internal and external forces; it also misses Newton’s third law (McKinsey et
al., 1953).

Real affine spaces Let us consider a structure A = (A, B, +), where A is a set
of points, B is a real8 vector space, and + : A × B → A. We define an operation
− : A × A → B such that for any vector x and any points P, Q, the following equivalence holds:
x + P = Q iﬀ Q − P = x.

It may also be convenient to write P⃗Q instead of Q − P ; we will be using both
notations.
Now A = (A, B, +) is a real affine space iff the following axioms are satisfied:
(1) 
For any points P, Q ∈ A, there exists exactly one vector x ∈ B such that
x = P⃗Q.
(2) For any points P, Q, R ∈ A,
⃗ = P⃗R.
P⃗Q + QR

An affine space A = (A, B, +) is said to be n-dimensional when B is an n-dimensional vector space.
Classical space-time structure Let A = (A, B, +) be a real four-dimensional affine
space. We define τ to be a mapping from A to the set of real numbers R, and we define
α to be a mapping from the range of τ to A. The τ function will be understood as a
mapping that provides the time of occurence of any space-time point-event in A, and
for any instant t, α(t) will be understood as the origin of the fixed inertial frame of reference. Thus, such (A, τ, α) is a classical space time structure iff for any P ∈ A, the set
{Q : τ (Q) = τ (P )} is a three-dimensional Euclidian space and τ (α(τ (P ))) = τ (P ).
The first requirement allows us to find the point-events that are simultaneous with any
point-event P . The second condition requires that “the origin of the inertial frame of
reference must be temporally present at all times” (Suppes, 2002, p. 319).9
For any t in the range of τ , we will understand A(t) as a three-dimensional real
affine subspace of A consisting of point-events occuring at time t.10
System of classical particle mechanics Now for any (A, τ, α), let:
● P be a nonempty set (understood as a set of particles),
● s : P × T → A (where T is the range of τ ; s is understood as a position

to consider which conditions are missing to unambigously distinguish inertial frames of reference from
non-intertial ones.

● g : P × T × N+ → B(3) (where N+ is the set of positive natural numbers that

We define an ordered five-tuple P = (P, s, m, f, g) to be a system of classical particle mechanics with respect to the classical space-time structure (A, τ, α) iff the
following axioms are satisfied:
1. The range of τ is a real interval.
2. The set P is finite and nonempty.
3. For any p ∈ P and any t ∈ T , s(p, t) ∈ A(t).
4. For any p ∈ P and any t ∈ T , the vector function s(p, t) − α(t) is twice differentiable at t.
5. For any p ∈ P , m(p) is a positive real number.
6. For any p, q ∈ P and t ∈ T ,
f (p, q, t) = −f (q, p, t).

f (p, q, t) − f (q, p, t), is equal to zero.

4 Defining determinism of CPM – the first approach
Suppes suggests that determinism in axiomatized CPM has already been established.
After presenting his formalization, he claims that by proving the following theorem,
it will be clear that “particle mechanics is thoroughly deterministic science”.
Theorem 1 Let P = (P, s, m, f , g) and P′ = (P, s ′ , m, f , g) be two systems of particle mechanics such that for some t0 in T and every p in P :

which a particle acts on itself is a zero-vector.

Then for every t in T and every p in P s(p, t) − α(t) = s ′ (p, t) − α(t). (Suppes,

Suppes does not define determinism explicitly, but his theorem reflects his interpretation. Two systems P and P′ are realizations and at some time t0 , the position
and velocity of any particle p are equal in both of them. Although it might seem that
Suppes’ approach is of a DMAP type, this intuition is misleading: except for the position function, in both realizations the functions m, f, g are assigned to be the same,
i.e. equal at any time. So, instead of assuming that the states are equal at some t, it is
assumed that except for the position function, they are equal at any t. Although Suppes does not prove Theorem 1, it is easy to come up with a proof that sheds light on
the triviality of such “determinism”:

As it can be seen, because of the strangely strong assumption that the forces are
equal in both models, Newton’s second law together with initial conditions yields
trivial “determinism”. Observe that neither of the approaches to DMAP analysis
presented in Sect. 2 allowed for assuming that some parameters are equal in both
realizations; in fact, this is what must be proven. It is only the initial conditions
(“realizations agreeing at one time”, “H1 (t) = H2 (t)”, or “two models that agree
at time t”) and the laws of the theory (which determine realizations, “the separate
possible ways a world could be”) that should be assumed in case of both models.18
A closely related approach is found in earlier literature. Examining his firstorder formalization of CPM, Montague (1974) defined the notion of determinism in
D1 , . . . Dk which is Laplacian determinism with an additional assumption that certain functions D1 , . . . Dk are equal in both models of a theory that are considered.19
In our case, CPM is deterministic in f and g . In Montague’s formalization with just
one function f representing the force, it also was shown that CPM is deterministic in
f by a reasoning similar to the above proof.
To restore meaningfulness of (in)determinism in CPM, we must apply a more standard DMAP analysis to Suppes’ formalization. However, we encounter an immediate
difficulty: so far there is no history function H that would be, as in the definition of
Laplacian determinism, “a map from R to tuples of values of the basic magnitudes”
(Earman, 2007, p. 1370). If there was such a function, we would take the following
steps: the family of those functions, a set {HA : A is a model of CPM}, would represent the class of temporal developments. Whenever we identify that two histories
18

One might be tempted to consider extending the domains of the functions representing forces to
f ∗ : P × P × A × A × T → B(3) and g ∗ : P × A × T × N+ → B(3) and modifying the axioms
to accomodate that change. One understanding of such an extension is that a single system’s history now
contains the underlying laws of physics: the functions g and f are capable of counterfactually describing
the force that would act on a particle p at time t if its position were different. Indeed, this way we would not
be able to prove Theorem 1. However, as the DMAP analysis requires placing individual realizations side
by side checking for divergence, a history should be a sequence of states, mapping time to the actual values
of basic physical magnitudes. When the force functions are turned into fields mapped over all of space A, a
realization is no longer a temporal development, but rather an entire universe equipped with a global force
field. We are skeptical whether such an approach allows for a meaningful DMAP-type analysis: both in
Montague’s and Suppes’ analyses, a single system represents a specific historical realization which admits
comparing divergent histories. A different option would be to adopt a compromise, defining
g ∗ (p, a, t, n) =

0

if sp (t) = a,
otherwise

and the f function in a similar way. However, it is easy to check that this would not prevent trivial determinism and Theorem 1 would still hold.
19

As we do not want to dive into the details of Montague’s formalization here, we are presenting a simplified (mostly with respect to notation and understanding of models) version of this definition. For details,
see Montague (1974, p. 322).

HA and HA′ admitted by a theory agree at some time t0 (i.e., the states H1 (t0 ) and
H2 (t0 ) are equal), we can check if they agree at all times t. If it is the case, then a
theory is deterministic; otherwise, we detect indeterminism.20
In the following section, it will be shown that such function can be found and that
the definition of Laplacian determinism can be applied to systems of CPM.

5 Defining determinism of CPM – the second approach
We now demonstrate how Laplacian determinism can be applied to Suppes’ version
of CPM. Again, most of the work has already been done by Montague, who described
how to build a function that Earman calls a history, H : R → S , where S are tuples of
basic physical magnitudes.21 We call S a set of states. For any t ∈ R that represents
an instant, the function H “gives a snapshot of the behavior of the basic magnitudes at time t” (Earman, 2007). Importantly, Montague showed how to extend this
function when the magnitudes are not simple functions of time. To build a relevant
function that applies to Suppes’ systems, we will follow his work (for details, see
Montague, 1974, p. 329).
Consider the structure P = (P, s, v, m, f, g). For convenience, we will write
gn (x, t) instead of g(x, t, n). We define:
SP = {(s(x1 , t) − α(t), v(x1 , t), m(x1 ), f (x1 , x2 , t), g1 (x1 , t), g2 (x1 , t) . . . ) : t ∈ T, x1 , x2 ∈ P }.

SP will be understood as the set of states, i.e. tuples of basic physical magnitudes.
We define a function stP : P 2 × T → SP such that for any t ∈ T and x1 , x2 ∈ P ,
the state of x1 , x2 at t is:
stP (x1 , x2 , t) = (s(x1 , t) − α(t), v(x1 , t), m(x1 ), f (x1 , x2 , t), g1 (x1 , t), g2 (x1 , t) . . . ). (6)

For the structure P and fixed t ∈ T we define the last auxiliary function
Ft : P 2 → SP such that for any x1 , x2 ∈ P , Ft (x1 , x2 ) = stP (x1 , x2 , t). We define
F = {Ft : t ∈ R} (the set of all Ft functions) and we finally define HP to be a function HP : T → F such that for any t ∈ T , HP (t) = Ft .22
These definitions are needed because Suppes’ functions depend on particles and
time, not just time. However, at the end of this procedure, we can obtain a function
that depends only on the time parameter.
Although obvious, it is important that each P determines a unique function.
20

Note that we slightly modify Earman’s definition. In his approach, we consider Hi functions indexed
by a natural that describe temporal development of a system (indeed, the name ‘history’ is accurate here)
and that are somehow admitted by a theory that we are describing. Now, to find such histories easier, it is
better to start with certain models of the theory; following Suppes’ formalization, they will be six-tuples
P = (P, s, v, m, f, g). For each such realization, we can then describe its temporal development by construing a relevant history function HP whose “source” is a certain model.

We can now examine whether CPM is deterministic. However, the following surprising result will eventually force us to change our approach.
Definition 2 (Laplacian determinism of CPM). Classical particle mechanics is Laplacian deterministic iff for any two systems of classical particle mechanics P and P′ ,
the following holds:
∀t0 , t ∈ T (HP (t0 ) = HP′ (t0 ) ⇒ HP (t) = HP′ (t)).

Taking two simple models with different force functions that coincide at one
moment yields a trivial form of indeterminism. The result lacks physical significance
because the functions, particularly the forces, are assigned arbitrarily. The verdict is
similar in Montague’s formalization: he claims that because of the possibility to take
arbitrary forces, it is “too obvious to include” the proof of the theorem that “[C]PM
is not deterministic”. Even with physically meaningful models, the definition permits
any two systems that briefly coincide to imply indeterminism.
In fact, it is probably this result on trivial indeterminism that led Montague to consider the definition of determinism in: he claims that “some authors make the more
cautious assertion that classical particle mechanics becomes deterministic once the
force-function is specified” (Montague, 1974, p. 330). But we have already seen that
“specifying” force by setting it equal in both considered models does not solve the
problem either. In the following section, it will be considered why those definitions
fail and how they can be corrected.

6 Physical frameworks and physical theories
To resolve this issue, we must distinguish between a physical framework and a physical theory. It should be noted that frameworks and theories will not be defined in
general in a clear-cut way; as Curiel (2021, pp. 4–7) shows, it is not obvious to find
criteria that will draw a sharp line between those two. However, despite this general difficulty, it seems possible to formalize the intuitions holding at least for CPM,
which will be the point of this section. This will enable us to find a way of applying
the definition of Laplacian determinism to CPM in a meaningful way.

13

247

Page 16 of 24

Synthese

(2026) 207:247

One idea of characterizing a framework was proposed by Friedman who describes
the relation between Newtonian laws of motion and more specific laws, such as the
law of gravitation, in the following way:
The privileged frame of reference in which the law of gravitation is defined is
what we now call an intertial frame, where an inertial frame of reference is simply one in which the Newtonian laws of motion hold … It follows that without
the Newtonian laws of mechanics the law of universal gravitation would not
even make empirical sense, let alone give a correct account of the empirical
phenomena … Once again, Newton’s mechanics and gravitational physics are
not happily viewed as symmetrically functioning elements of a larger conjunction: the former is rather a necessary part of the language or conceptual framework within which alone the latter makes empirical sense. (Friedman, 2001,
pp. 36–37)
Here, Newtonian framework is meant to distinguish inertial frames from non-inertial
ones. In our formalization, it is the function α that is a part of classical space-time
and which provides ‘the origin of the fixed inertial frame of reference’. In contrast to
this approach, Curiel believes that what distinguishes a framework from a theory is
the following:
Newtonian mechanics, the heart of which is embodied in the definitions and the
three laws Newton lays out in his Principia, is a framework. Newton’s Second
Law in the abstract is not the equation of motion of any particular kind of physical system. It is rather the schema that any equation of motion for any particular
kind of system treated by the framework must instantiate. Newton’s theory of
gravity is a theory formulated in the framework of Newtonian mechanics. It
treats that kind of physical system characterized, inter alia, by the possession of
inertial mass, gravitational mass, spatial position, and a velocity expressible as
the temporal derivative of spatial position, all such that the system’s dynamical
evolution is governed by Newton’s gravitational force law. (Curiel, 2021, p. 5)
The mention of Newton’s gravitational force law is crucial. In the physical framework of Newtonian mechanics, we are given only a very general constraint for the
force (embodied in Newton’s third law) in any system. A theory of such a system
contains an equation governing the behavior of a force. Informally, a framework of
CPM is then a set of sentences that are necessary conditions that must be satisfied
by any P to be a system of classical particle mechanics; in our formalization, those
sentences are the nine axioms given in Sect. 3. A theory is then a framework enriched
with additional axioms that, by Curiel words, “allow for the unified representation
and modeling of a particular kind of physical system”.23 This idea appears in the
23

Curiel characterizes frameworks and theories mostly by giving some examples; another theory of
Newtonian mechanics is Navier-Stokes theory. He also mentions other frameworks: special relativity,
non-relativistic quantum mechanics, and quantum field theory; their theories are, respectively: theory of
classical Maxwell fields, the atomic theory of elements of low atomic weight, and quantum electrodynamics (Curiel, 2021, 6).

13

Synthese

(2026) 207:247

Page 17 of 24

247

work of Montague (1974), where extra axioms transform CPM into a gravitational
theory. Importantly, one of those axioms incorporates an equation for gravitational
force, i.e. a law of gravitation, so that the force function can no longer be defined
arbitrarily. From the above observations, it is clear that for any framework F and its
theory T (if they are both definitions of set-theoretical predicates), the models of the
theory T should be a subset of the models of the framework F , so any system of a
certain theory would be a system of its framework.
It is interesting to consider what may appear in such a theory. Definitely, the force
equation and the equation of motion must be present; while Curiel (2021, pp. 6–7)
stresses the importance of the latter, in our case it is given by Axiom 9. We may also
ask about the constants that appear in those equations. In an example of a harmonic
oscillator given by Curiel, we can fix the constants that appear in its equation of
k
x, for instance by setting k = 5 and m = 1. Also, we might set a
motion x′′ = − m
√
k
t).
solution to the generic equation of motion, for example by fixing x(t) = cos( m

Obviously, in our case, it is not reasonable to fix a solution to the equation of motion
as we want to examine whether a theory admits more than one such solution (which
signals indeterminism).
Note that although the distinction between frameworks and theories and, particularly, between different levels of theories is not sharp, it seems that applying the
definition of determinism to a theory rather than a framework fixes the problem of
setting an arbitrary force (and so the equation of motion) that signals unmeaningful
indeterminism, as it was done in the proof of Theorem 3. In particular, we can consider a theory with a given force equation, fix the initial conditions and then examine
whether there is only one possible evolution of a system. If it happens that the equation admits more than one evolution, it signals that the class of systems described by
a theory is indeterministic. From now on, we will follow this approach.
The important point here is that the equation of the force is admitted by the framework; not only does it have to be consistent with the axioms constituting a framework,
but also it has to be somehow “physical”; for example, it should not be dependent on
some contingent qualities such as naming of the particles.24 Distinguishing proper
theories from, as Norton puts it, pathological ones is fundamental but difficult, and
lies beyond this paper’s scope.
In the case of classical particle mechanics, there seems to be a general agreement among both philosophers and physicists on how to distinguish theories from a
framework, although different naming conventions for that are adopted. For example,
Wilson (2013, p. 12) claims that while Newton’s laws provide the “basic scaffolding” of classical mechanics, “we must yet specify the sundry fi (j, t) in concrete
ways”; Wilson calls such an equation “a special force law”. In his classic textbook
on Newtonian mechanics, Arnold (1989, p. 8) states that Newton’s equations form
the laws and “the form of function F”, determined experimentally, “constitutes the
definition of [a] system”. Finally, Feynman et al. (2011) puts it shortly: “in order to
use Newton’s laws, we have to have some formula for the force; these laws say pay
attention to the forces”.
24

For different ways in which theory might be ‘unphysical’, see Norton (2008).

13

247

Page 18 of 24

Synthese

(2026) 207:247

Based on those observations, we can formulate the following definitions:
Definition 3 (Framework of CPM). The framework of classical particle mechanics is
the definition of a set-theoretical predicate “is a system of classical particle mechanics”. Any tuple that satisfies this predicate is a system of classical particle mechanics.
Definition 4 (Theory of CPM). The conjunction of the framework of classical particle mechanics with the formulas from the set Θ (stated in the language of set theory)
is a theory of classical particle mechanics iff:
● it defines a set-theoretical predicate,
● it is consistent,
● there exist β ∈ Θ, γ ∈ Θ of the form:
i) β ≡ ∀p, q ∈ P ∀t ∈ T f (p, q, t) = βterm ,
ii) γ ≡ ∀p ∈ P ∀t ∈ T ∀n ∈ N+ g(p, t, n) = γterm ,
where βterm , γterm are terms in the language of set theory with at most p, q, t and
p, t, n variables free, respectively.25  
Any tuple that satisfies the predicate defined by a theory of CPM is a system of a
theory of classical particle mechanics.
It seems meaningless to ask whether a framework of CPM is deterministic or indeterministic per se. Rather, we should ask whether a framework admits indeterministic
theories, i.e. whether the theories of indeterministic physical systems can be formulated within the framework. Usually, our verdict will depend on the differential equation of motion that will appear in the theory. A proper way to examine determinism
would again be to follow the definition of Laplacian determinism: we have to take
two systems admitted by the theory such that their initial conditions are the same. If
there is more than one way of evolution of such a system, the theory is indeterministic; otherwise, it is deterministic.
Definition 5 (Laplacian determinism of framework). A framework is Laplacian
deterministic iff its every theory is deterministic.
Definition 6 (Laplacian determinism of the theories of CPM). A theory of classical
particle mechanics is Laplacian deterministic iff for any two of its models P and P′ ,
the following holds:
∀t0 , t ∈ T (HP (t0 ) = HP′ (t0 ) ⇒ HP (t) = HP′ (t)).
25

While our analysis is confined to the idealized framework of CPM, we acknowledge that a more physically realistic ontology could incorporate interacting physical fields (e.g., classical electromagnetic fields)
to account for interaction mechanisms and momentum conservation. However, this might not be consistent
with the axioms defining the framework, for example Axiom 6, so Θ cannot contain such formulae in all
cases.

13

Synthese

(2026) 207:247

Page 19 of 24

247

We can use those definitions to finally assess whether CPM is deterministic. Note
that we do not allow taking different interpretations of the force parameter that led to
trivial indeterminism of CPM. We neither “set” the forces in any models of a theory
to be equal; we are not interested in the flawed notion of determinism in. Instead, we
consider if the differential equation, if it appears in a theory, admits different solutions. This way we reflect the intuition behind the DMAP approach that “the practical
assessment of determinism or indeterminism of a given theory mostly depends on the
behaviour of that theory’s defining differential equations” (Müller & Placek, 2018,
p. 226).

7 Defining determinism of CPM – the third approach
We now use the revised method to demonstrate indeterminism in CPM. We will apply
the definition to a system of CPM known as Norton’s (2008) dome, where the equation of motion of a particle violates the Lipschitz condition (sufficient for the existence of a unique solution). Müller and Placek (2018, pp. 232–234) argue that all
major approaches (including DMAP) classify Norton’s dome as indeterministic.

(38)

g(a, 0, 1) = g ′ (a, 0, 1) = (0, 0, 0), so HP (0) = HP′ (0).

29

This construction is necessary because Definition 4 requires γterm to be a strictly set-theoretic term. A
standard piecewise definition is a formula rather than a term and we reflect this conditional logic by defining G as a set of ordered pairs. The first subset of G encodes the force equation of the dome by collapsing
the cases for x ≥ 0 and x < 0 into a single algebraic expression using the signum function. The second
subset ensures that for n > 1, the force is the zero vector, which is required to set other external forces to
zero. Evaluating G at the argument π1 (s(p, t) − α(t)) returns a (signed) square root of the position of
a particle at time t. This example is not only crucial for our further analysis, but also shows that β and γ
might be complex formulas encoding quite sophisticated force equations.

clude that HP (0) = HP′ (0) and HP (2) ̸= HP′ (2), so this theory is not deterministic. As the theory of Norton’s domes is a theory within the framework of classical
particle mechanics, we conclude that CPM is not Laplacian deterministic. 
□

8 Conclusions
Recall the quotes of Montague and Suppes given in the introduction: while Montague
believed that classical particle mechanics is not deterministic, Suppes claimed that
it is a “throughly deterministic science”. Our analysis indicates that neither author’s
conclusion is fully adequate. Suppes’ definition is too strong because it assumes
identical forces in both models. This motivates revising the definition and adopting a DMAP-style analysis; however, even when applied correctly, DMAP does not
meaningfully assess the entire CPM framework. Meaningful results arise only when
DMAP is applied to specific theories of CPM such as the theory of Norton’s domes.
In this case, the verdict is similar as it was in the analysis suggested by Müller and

13

Synthese

(2026) 207:247

Page 23 of 24

247

Placek (2018, pp. 232–234), and Norton himself (2008) – if the theory of Norton’s
domes is stated within the framework of CPM, we can prove that classical particle
mechanics is not deterministic.
The fundamental distinction between frameworks and theories reaches beyond
CPM and can be applied to other physical concepts. The moral from the formally
simple example of assessing determinism of CPM should be the following: whenever
we consider determinism of any physical theory, not only do we have to construct a
philosophically adequate and formally rigorous definition of determinism, but also
we must specify how such a definition can be used. We argued that the general constraint is that determinism of a framework should be dependent on determinism of
each of its theories, so a DMAP-type analysis must be applied to the particular theories that describe different physical systems.
However, in the general case the framework–theory distinction remains informally defined. Stressing the importance of this distinction in the case of defining
determinism, we leave for future work a difficult task to find the relevant philosophical, physical, and logical criteria for distinguishing between frameworks and theories
that may be crucial to consider determinism of other (possible) frameworks such as
quantum mechanics.

argument.
